activity.title: I just had the craziest week of my life in SF. 🌉 Firstly, I got accepted into the Founders, Inc. OffSeason 2 batch! I genuinely wasn't ready for what that first week would feel like. The founders in that room are building things I couldn't have imagined: people from all over the world, going after problems at a scale that's hard to wrap your head around. Non-stop —back-to-back sessions, late nights, big ideas, learning from people further along than I've ever been around. Pushing myself harder than I ever have. This is the next step in my journey as a founder, and I'm only just getting started. I also had the chance to have lunch with Matt Curl , the CEO of Apollo, after winning first place at the Apollo.io x Google Cloud Hackathon! During our lunch we talked about his path as an entrepreneur, what it actually looks like to build in this industry, the real lessons, the hard advice. Genuinely one of the best conversations I've had as a founder. So grateful for the mentorship, and for the chance to keep growing my network with people like Matt. (Thanks for the yummy food 😋) Next few weeks are going to be absolutely crazy. Stay tuned 🚀 ...more

We just won the Most Creative Project at the Cursor x a16z speedrun Hackathon yesterday. 🎉 What we built: Specter. Say you want to edit YouTube videos but have no idea how to use DaVinci Resolve. Normally you're stuck googling tutorials or asking ChatGPT, then trying to translate that into actual clicks on your actual screen. Specter skips that gap. It's an AI agent that lives on your computer, watches your screen, and talks you through whatever app you're in, in real time. Ask it how to do something and it guides you right there in the software, step by step, instead of sending you off to figure it out yourself. It also remembers. Specter keeps a local memory of what you've learned and where you left off, so it's not starting from scratch every time you open the app. The bigger goal: make any application learnable this way, so people outside the engineering world can pick up real tools fast instead of bouncing between tabs trying to piece it together. Huge thanks to Eric Zakariasson , Baltazar Zuñiga Ruiz , Sunita Rao , Shub G. , and Yoko Li for hosting an amazing event! Most of all, loved building this with my teammates Rohan Garg , Bhagirath Reddy Bandigari , and Aarush Tahiliani couldn't have done it without you. ...more

I just won the Apollo.io x Google Cloud Hackathon last thursday. 🎉 What I built: ARIA, an autonomous revenue intelligence agent that automates the entire SDR loop across six specialized AI systems. How it works: → Apollo.io finds and enriches the right prospects → Gemini researches live signals on every lead → 3 Claude agents debate targeting strategy before anyone gets called → Vapi + ElevenLabs conducts the personalized cold call → Post-call: meeting recaps sent, data logged to Sheets, team notified on Slack → A self-learning reinforcement model analyzes every call and refines the approach over time No SDR team. No manual research. No switching between tools. Just drop a domain. ARIA closes the loop, then gets better at closing it. The piece that felt genuinely new: the system does not stop when the call ends. It studies what worked, updates its targeting strategy, and improves the next run. That is not a pipeline. That is an agent that compounds. This is what agentic outbound actually looks like when the right primitives are wired together. Huge thanks to Anshul Pahwa and Xi-Er Dang for hosting, and to Apollo.io and Google for making this possible. Congrats to all the other winners and participants! #AI #Apollo #GoogleCloud #Hackathon #RevenueIntelligence #SalesAgents ...more

If you're anything like me and run multiple AI coding agents at once, steal this. I usually have 3 or 4 Antigravity (currently my IDE of choice) windows open, each with its own agent grinding away in a terminal. They all look identical. More than once I've typed a command into the wrong project. The fix took two minutes: color-code each window. Drop a settings.json file in each project's .vscode folder and you can set the title bar, status bar, and activity bar to whatever color you want. Purple is The Postinator. Blue is a client project. Green is Ivy and Oak, the experiment I'll probably delete. (Kidding, John Pace Mostly.) Now I can tell at a glance which agent is doing what, even from across the room. Works in VS Code, Cursor, Antigravity, any of the forks. I'll put the config snippet in the comments. What's your trick for juggling multiple agent sessions?

The biggest question in audit AI right now is the wrong one. "Will this cut hours on our control testing?" And while the answer is yes, it's a question shaped by the first generation of AI tools. This was chat and basic workflow automation, where you paste in a control description, upload data, and the AI tells you what happened. The better question is how much of your company you actually see, and whether you see it in time to fix what's broken. That's the new generation of AI-enabled assurance, where agents sit across hundreds of enterprise applications year round, build persistent memory of how a company's control environment operates, and continuously test the whole population instead of a 1% sample. Issues surface and get remediated in the month they happen, before they compound into a material weakness, a disclosure, and an external audit fee that goes up the next year. That's the real cost of an audit. Hours are the small part. Every audit leader we work with describes some version of this when you ask what their team would do if they weren't buried in manual work all year. Audit becomes the control plane of the enterprise, and we're building Arden (YC P26) to be the infrastructure that powers it.

I'm 17, and I moved to San Francisco alone to fix the thing that killed my best friend. Two years ago, he died in a building collapse in India. Rescue took three days to search the rubble. Drones were on site, but every drone needed its own pilot, and nobody had one picture of what had already been searched. He was alive under there for part of it. So I've spent the last month building software where one person runs an entire robot fleet. When a machine dies mid-job, the nearest one picks up its unfinished work. Everything is logged and replayable, so when someone asks what actually happened, you can prove it instead of guessing. And it turns out this was never just a drone problem. Mining machines, forklifts, farm robots, every fleet hits the same wall the moment one machine drops. If you build or operate robot fleets, I'd genuinely love to hear how you handle a machine dying mid-job. My DMs are open.

I built a game where the speedrun timer is your startup's runway. SF SPEEDRUN a pixel platformer about surviving SF startup culture: - standing still burns money (this is SF) - your MOM can be your co-founder, she leads your seed when you hit $0 - hire a corgi as Chief Morale Officer (multiplies your valuation, obviously) - you can pick your pedigree: (ex-Stanfurd, ex-AI lab, or self made) - dying prints your obituary in a startup newspaper - win under $1B and you're stamped CERTIFIED HORSE 🐴 One HTML file. No engine. No assets. Built with Claude Code. It becomes a Game Boy on your phone. I've never launched anything before, this went live this morning and it's at ~1,300 players. On Saturday I'm at YC Startup School, so the timing felt right. Top scorer in the next 30 days gets 6 months of Claude Pro. check out sfspeedrun.com
